sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Valemetostat tosylate (valemetostat) is an oral, selective, dual inhibitor of enhancer of zeste homolog (EZH)2 and EZH1. This article reports findings on the mass balance and pharmacokinetics of valemetostat in a phase I study; valemetostat metabolite identification in plasma, urine, and fecal samples; and plasma-protein-binding of valemetostat in vitro.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Eight healthy participants received a single 200-mg oral dose of [14C]-valemetostat under fasting conditions. Blood, urine, and feces samples were collected to determine total radioactivity and/or unchanged valemetostat, and for metabolite identification. The binding of valemetostat 600–10,000 ng/mL to plasma, 4% human serum albumin (HSA), and 0.1% alpha-1-acid glycoprotein (AAG) was assessed in vitro.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Mean cumulative recovery of administered radioactivity was 95.3% by 360 h post-dose, with a mean recovery of 15.6% in urine and 79.8% in feces. Valemetostat accounted for the most radioactivity in the excreta, at 10% and 64.9% of the administered dose in the urine and feces, respectively. CALZ-1809a was the most abundant metabolite, present in all biological samples, and accounted for 5.6% of total radioactivity in the feces. Valemetostat was minimally associated with red blood cells, with a blood-to-plasma total radioactivity ratio of 0.54. In vitro, valemetostat was highly plasma-bound (> 94%) at clinically relevant concentrations, with a higher affinity to AAG than to HSA.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Valemetostat was rapidly absorbed into the systemic circulation, mainly excreted via the biliary/fecal route, primarily metabolized by CYP3A enzymes to CALZ-1809a, and highly bound to plasma proteins, with a greater affinity to AAG than HSA in vitro.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Valemetostat tosylate (valemetostat) is an oral, selective, dual inhibitor of enhancer of zeste homolog (EZH)2 and EZH1 under clinical investigation for the treatment of non-Hodgkin lymphomas (NHLs), including peripheral T-cell lymphoma (PTCL), adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL), and solid tumors [1–5]. EZH2 and its close homolog EZH1 are histone methyltransferases that catalyze the trimethylation of histone H3 at lysine 27 (H3K27me3) [6–7]. Dual inhibition of EZH2 and EZH1 by valemetostat suppresses H3K27me3; suppression of H3K27me3 results in consequent down-regulation of gene transcription pathways involved in tumor cell proliferation, progression, and migration [8–9].

In the first-in-human, phase 1, dose-escalation and -expansion trial in patients with R/R B- or T-cell NHLs (DS3201-A-J101; NCT02732275), valemetostat 200 mg/day (continuous 28-day cycles) was shown to be safe, well-tolerated, and clinically active, and was thus chosen as the recommended phase 2 dose [10]. Valemetostat was associated with an objective response rate of 48.0% in a phase 2, single-arm trial comprising 25 Japanese patients with R/R ATLL (DS3201-A-J201; NCT04102150), an aggressive T-cell lymphoma subtype with limited treatment options [11]. Based on the results of this trial valemetostat was approved in Japan in September 2022 for the treatment of R/R ATLL.

The efficacy and safety of valemetostat 200 mg/day was further assessed in patients with R/R PTCL, and safety in patients with R/R ATLL, in the multicenter, single-arm, open-label, phase 2 VALENTINE-PTCL01 trial (DS3201-A-U202; NCT04703192); patients with R/R PTCLs achieved an objective response rate of 43.7% (52/133) [12], leading to the approval of valemetostat for the treatment of R/R PTCL in Japan in June 2024.

The clinical pharmacokinetics (PK) of valemetostat have been studied in healthy participants and in patients with R/R NHL. In healthy participants receiving a single valemetostat oral dose (50 to 200 mg) under fasting conditions, the maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) and area under the concentration–time curve (AUC) were generally dose-proportional [13]. At 200 mg, the mean Cmax and median time to Cmax (Tmax) was 1500 ng/mL and 4.5 h, respectively. After reaching Cmax, valemetostat plasma concentrations declined with a mean apparent terminal elimination half-life (t1/2) of approximately 20 h. Valemetostat is highly protein bound in human plasma with the mean fraction unbound value ranging from 0.04 to 0.06 [13]. In the valemetostat population PK analysis, baseline alpha-1 acid glycoprotein (AAG) was the most influential covariate on total valemetostat exposure, with higher AAG levels associated with increased exposure, whereas baseline AAG had little impact on unbound valemetostat exposure [14].

In a phase 1 study in patients with NHL, following once daily oral dose administration of valemetostat, the median Tmax was 2–4 h across the 150–300 mg tested dose range [10]. Valemetostat showed high inter-participant variability in exposure (the percentage coefficient of variation for total valemetostat Cmax and AUC from time 0 to tau [24 h] on cycle 1 day 15 was > 70%). In a phase 2 study in patients with NHLs, accumulation of valemetostat after once daily dosing was minimal with a mean accumulation ratio of 1.19 at 200 mg [11].

In vitro, valemetostat is metabolized by cytochrome P450 (CYP)3A4 and CYP3A5, and to a lesser extent, by CYP2C8 [Data on file]. CALZ-1809a is the major metabolite of valemetostat, and its formation is mediated by CYP3A enzymes. Valemetostat was also identified as a substrate for P-glycoprotein. When valemetostat was co-administered with itraconazole (a strong CYP3A inhibitor and P-glycoprotein inhibitor), valemetostat Cmax and AUC extrapolated to infinity (AUCinf) were increased, with a geometric least square mean ratio of 2.9 for Cmax and 4.2 for AUCinf compared to valemetostat alone [15].

In this phase 1 study, the absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME) of valemetostat was investigated in healthy male adults following a single 200 mg radiolabeled [14C] dose. To support and contextualize the ADME data, in vitro protein binding of valemetostat to plasma proteins was explored.

The objectives of these studies included: assessment of the recovery of [14C]-valemetostat by quantification of the total [14C] radioactivity in urine and feces; determination of the PK of total [14C] radioactivity in whole blood and plasma; determination of valemetostat and CALZ-1809a PK in plasma; determination of the metabolite profile in plasma, urine, and feces; and determination of the safety and tolerability of valemetostat; determination of the binding ratio of valemetostat to plasma proteins (in vitro).

sec.title: Chemicals and standards
sec.p: Unlabeled valemetostat, [2H6]-valemetostat, and reference standards for the metabolites CALZ-1808a, CALZ-1809a, and CALZ-1810a were synthesized by Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd. [2H6]-CALZ-1809a was synthesized by HepatoChem Inc. [14C]-valemetostat was manufactured by EAG Laboratories. All other chemicals and reagents were obtained from commercial suppliers and were of analytical grade.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: This single-center, open-label, single-dose, phase 1 study (DS3201-A-U105) evaluated the ADME profile, PK, safety, and tolerability of [14C]-valemetostat in healthy male participants. The study was performed at Covance Clinical Research Unit (Madison, WI), and was conducted in compliance with the protocol, the ethical principles that have their origin in the Declaration of Helsinki, the International Conference on Harmonisation, consolidated Guideline E6 for Good Clinical Practice, and applicable regulatory requirements. The protocol, amendment, letter of administrative change, and informed consent were approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB).

sec.title: Participants
sec.p: Healthy male participants 18–55 years of age with a body mass index of ≥ 19.0 and < 30.0 kg/m2 were enrolled. The health status was confirmed through medical history, physical examination, 12-lead electrocardiogram, and clinical laboratory evaluations. Exclusion criteria included use of selected drugs of abuse or any medications; positivity for the hepatitis panel and human immunodeficiency virus; history or current evidence of malignancies, cardiac, hepatic, renal, pulmonary, endocrine, neurologic, infectious, gastrointestinal, hematologic, or oncologic disease; and exposure to radiations.

sec.title: Dose preparation/schedule
sec.p: Each participant received a single oral dose of 200 mg valemetostat containing approximately 150 µCi of 14C-radiolabeled valemetostat. The selected 200-mg dose was established as the recommended phase 2 dose in the first-in-human phase 1 clinical trial (DS3201-A-J101) [10]. At this dose, valemetostat was shown to be safe and well tolerated among healthy participants prior to the initiation of this study [13].

The radioactive dose of approximately 150 µCi was considered an acceptable dose for humans in 14C-labeled drug metabolism studies of this type based on quantitative whole-body autoradiography studies using male Sprague Dawley and Long-Evans (pigmented) rats [16]. The overall whole-body radiation dose in human male participants following the administration of a single 150 µCi (5.55 MBq) dose of [14C]-valemetostat was calculated to be 26.6 mrem (0.266 mSv), which is well below the US Food and Drug Administration exposure limit of 3000 mrem (30 mSv) for a single dose in human isotope studies [17].

The final dose formulation for oral administration was prepared at the study site by dissolving the powdered [14C]-valemetostat in sterile water to a concentration of approximately 4 mg/mL (3 µCi/mL). The dose contained approximately 5.55 MBq (0.266 mSv) of radioactivity, which is within the acceptable range as set by the International Commission on Radiological Protection guidelines for category IIa studies (0.1–1 mSv) [18].

Eligible participants were admitted 24 h prior to the drug administration and were kept for overnight fasting lasting at least 8 h. Participants remained seated for 4 h after dosing and were restricted from caffeinated beverages, grape-fruit juice, alcohol, and concomitant medications. Participants were discharged after sample collections on study day 8 if≥ 90% of the radioactive dose was recovered and if urine and fecal sample collections over three consecutive 24-hour days each contained < 1% of the administered radioactivity. If these radioactivity recovery criteria were not met by study day 8, blood, urine, and fecal samples were collected daily, and participants were discharged from the clinic once radioactivity recovery criteria were met. Participants were discharged by day 22 even if the radioactivity recovery criteria were not met, with return visits to the clinic every 48 or 72 h thereafter until the remaining radioactivity in plasma was undetectable, or up to study day 31, whichever occurred first (Supplementary Fig. 1).

sec.title: Sample collection
sec.p: Blood samples (8 mL) were collected for determination of total radioactivity and PK analyses of valemetostat and CALZ-1809a (a major oxidized metabolite of valemetostat) at pre-dose and at 0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 12, 24, 36, 48, 72, 96, 120, 144, and 168 h post-dose. Approximately 1 mL from each blood collection was used for determination of whole blood radioactivity, and the remaining blood was used to separate plasma. Blood samples (10 mL) for metabolite identification were drawn at 0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 12, and 24 h post-dose. Urine was collected before dosing and at 0–12, 12–24, 24–48, 48–72, 72–96, 96–120, 120–144, and 144–168 h post-dose. One 10-mL aliquot was used for determination of radioactivity, and another two 10-mL aliquots were used for metabolite identification. Fecal samples were collected pre-dose, then at 0–24, 24–48, 48–72, 72–96, 96–120, 120–144, and 144–168 h post-dose. Feces samples of each participant were combined at 24-hour intervals, weighed, and homogenized with water. Duplicate weighed aliquots (approximately 0.2 g) were used for determination of radioactivity and duplicate 50 g subsamples were retained for metabolite identification. All aliquots and/or subsamples were stored at − 70 ℃ until used for further analysis. Additional collections were performed beyond 168 h if radioactivity recovery criteria for discharge had not been met.

sec.title: Determination of total radioactivity
sec.p: Blood, plasma, urine, and feces samples were mixed, and duplicate weighed aliquots (approximately 0.2 g) were analyzed for content of radioactivity by liquid scintillation counter (LSC), with blood and feces combusted prior to analysis.

sec.title: Determination of valemetostat and CALZ-1809a in plasma
sec.p: Plasma concentrations of valemetostat and CALZ-1809a were determined by ultra-high performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) equipped with an AB SCIEX triple quadrupole mass spectrometer, API 4000™ for detection of valemetostat, and API 5000™ for detection of CALZ-1809a. An aliquot of human plasma (K2EDTA) containing the analyte and internal standard was extracted using a protein precipitation procedure. Quantitation was done using a weighted linear regression analysis (1/concentration2) of peak area ratios of the analyte and internal standard. The lower limit of quantitation was 20 ng/mL and 1 ng/mL for valemetostat and CALZ-1809a, respectively.

sec.title: PK assessments
sec.p: The cumulative percentage of the dose excreted in the urine and feces was assessed based on the radioactivity measured in each sample. The PK parameters for total radioactivity in whole blood and plasma included estimation of Cmax, Tmax, AUC from time 0 to 24 h post-dose (AUC0 − 24 h), AUC from time 0 to the time of last measurable concentration (AUClast), AUCinf, and whole blood to plasma ratios for total radioactivity with respect to Cmax, AUClast, and AUCinf.

The PK parameters for valemetostat and CALZ-1809a in the plasma included, estimation of Cmax, Tmax; AUC0 − 24 h; AUClast; AUCinf; t1/2; apparent total body clearance and apparent volume of distribution based on the terminal phase (valemetostat only); plasma ratios of metabolite CALZ-1809a to valemetostat with respect to Cmax, AUClast, and AUCinf; and ratios of valemetostat to total radioactivity with respect to Cmax, AUClast, and AUCinf. The noncompartmental PK analyses for total radioactivity, valemetostat and its metabolites were performed using WinNonlin, version 8.1 (Certara, US, Inc.).

sec.title: Quantification and characterization of metabolites
sec.p: Biological samples were analyzed for identification, quantification, and structural elucidation of metabolites using HPLC + LSC and liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) systems. As plasma samples around Cmax were missing for 1 participant (1001-0001) due to limited volumes obtained by venipuncture, two different samples were prepared for metabolite analysis described in Supplementary Table 1; an equal volume of plasma samples at various time points from participant 1001-0001 were pooled (Plasma 1), and plasma samples at Cmax from various participants (1001-0002 to 0008) were equally pooled (Plasma 2). For metabolite analysis in urine and feces, each individual samples were pooled at the time intervals shown in Supplementary Table 1. Exactly 2 mL of each pooled sample was then weighed, mixed with 3-fold volume of acetonitrile, shaken (10 min), centrifuged (1800 × g, 4℃, 10 min), and the supernatant was collected. The residue was extracted twice by suspending in water (the same volume of the sample), mixed with 3-fold volume of acetonitrile, shaken, and centrifuged in the same manner. All the three supernatants were combined and subjected to radiochromatographic analyses. The recovery of radioactivity (%) through sample processing, the recovery of radioactivity (%) during HPLC analysis of each sample, and the excretion (% of dose) in the urine and feces were calculated.

Radiochromatographic analyses of processed biological samples were performed using an HPLC system (Shimadzu; Kyoto, Japan). The HPLC column of 3 μm was passed with mobile phase A (0.1% formic acid in water) and B (0.1% formic acid in acetonitrile) in a gradient manner at a flow rate of 1 mL/min.

The HPLC eluate of the biological samples were fractionated at 18 s intervals using a fraction collector (RETRIEVER IV; Teledyne Isco, Lincoln, NE). The radioactivity of each fraction was measured by LSC (2500 TR, 2700 TR, 3100 TR, or 3110 TR; PerkinElmer; Waltham, MA). Radiochromatograms of each sample were reported using Microsoft Office Excel (versions 2010 and 2016, Microsoft, Redmond, WA). Radioactive peaks corresponding to [14C]-valemetostat and its metabolites were identified and quantified from the radiochromatograms. Radioactivity concentrations were converted to valemetostat (ng eq. of valemetostat/mL). The lower limit of quantification was designated as 1.0%, values below this were considered not detectable. Metabolite profiling was performed using LTQ Orbitrap XL system (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA). The structure of each metabolite was identified or estimated using the data obtained from analysis of each sample. The LC–MS/MS system was equipped with an electrospray interface and was operated using the positive ion detection mode. Chemical structures of [14C]-valemetostat and its metabolites detected as radioactive peaks were identified by comparing the respective retention times, molecular weights, molecular formulae, and tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) spectra to those of the authentic standards. Ultraviolet and mass chromatograms of a mixed authentic standard solution were reported using Xcalibur v2.1.0 (Thermo Fisher Scientific; Waltham, MA). Chemical structures of metabolites that did not match with any authentic standard were elucidated from the MS (MS/MS) spectra. Representative MS (MS/MS) spectra of each metabolite were reported using Xcalibur.

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: Safety assessments were conducted by recording treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs), clinical laboratory assessments (clinical chemistry, hematology, coagulation parameters, and urinalysis), vital signs (pulse rate, blood pressure, oral body temperature, and respiratory rate), electrocardiograms, and physical examinations. TEAEs were graded according to the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0.

sec.title: Statistical assessments
sec.p: The sample size of eight participants was not based on any statistical consideration but was considered sufficient to assess the recovery of [14C]-valemetostat. Data are summarized statistically and represented as mean ± SD.

sec.title: In vitro protein binding assessment
sec.p: Plasma, 4% human serum albumin (HSA), and 0.1% AAG were each fortified with valemetostat to reach a final concentration of 600, 1000, 3000, 5000, and 10,000 ng/mL. Solutions were ultracentrifuged (OptimaTM MAX, Beckman Coulter, Inc.) at 627,000 × g for 160 min at 4 ℃ and the middle supernatant layer was retained and analyzed by LC–MS/MS for valemetostat concentration. Each experiment was done in triplicate.

For total concentration measurement, samples were prepared for LC–MS/MS by mixing an aliquot of plasma, 4% HSA or 0.1% AAG; acetonitrile; and an internal standard (500 ng/mL [2H6]-valemetostat) and centrifuged at 13,000 × g for 2 minutes at 4 ℃. The supernatant was collected and mixed with 5 mmol/L ammonium formate containing 0.01% formic acid. For unbound concentration measurement, samples were prepared for LC–MS/MS by mixing an aliquot of plasma, 4% HSA or 0.1% AAG supernatant; internal standard (25 ng/mL [2H6]-valemetostat); 5 mmol/L ammonium formate containing 0.01% formic acid; and acetonitrile. Valemetostat was separated on an OSAKA SODA CO., LTD. C18 column (2.0 mm 2.0 mm × 50 mm internal diameter × 50 mm, particle size 3 μm) in a mobile phase of 5 mmol/L ammonium formate containing 0.01% formic acid (phase A) and acetonitrile (phase B). Samples were eluted with a gradient increasing of phase B/phase A from 80:20 to 5:95, then back to 80:20. The total analytical run time was 5 min, and the flow rate was 0.5 mL/min. Detection was performed by tandem mass spectrometer (API5000; AB SCIEX), which was operated in the positive ion detection mode. Multiple reaction monitoring was used for quantification.

sec.title: Enrolment, participant demographics, and safety
sec.p: Eight male participants were enrolled and received a single dose of 200 mg [14C]-valemetostat on day 1, providing a total radioactive dose of 150 µCi. At screening, the mean (SD) age and body mass index of the enrolled participants were 38.3 (9.7) years and 27.9 (2.38) kg/m2, respectively (Supplementary Table 2). All eight participants completed the study in accordance with the protocol and were included in the PK and safety analyses. [14C]-valemetostat at 200 mg was well tolerated with appearance of Grade 1 TEAEs in four participants (50%). Reported TEAEs were diarrhea in two participants; and rectal hemorrhage, vessel puncture site hemorrhage, skin laceration, and pain in extremity in one participant each. One case of diarrhea was considered to be related to valemetostat treatment and no serious TEAEs were reported.

sec.title: PK of radioactivity in excreta
sec.p: After oral administration of a single dose of 200 mg [14C]-valemetostat, approximately 95% of the total administered radioactive dose was recovered over the 360-hour study, with a mean recovery of 86.7% (15.3% in urine and 71.4% in feces) at 96 h post-dose and 90% at 120 h post-dose (Fig. 1).

sec.p: The observed mean recoveries of total radioactivity in urine and feces were 15.6% and 79.8%, respectively (Table 1). All participants met both discharge criteria at 120-hours post-dose, i.e., achieving ≥ 90% of total radioactive dose recovery and < 1% of total radioactive dose recovery in samples from three consecutive 24-hour intervals (Supplementary Fig. 1). Radioactivity in the urine was quantifiable through at least 120 h post-dose, and small amounts of radioactivity were still quantifiable in feces of all participants up to the time of discharge.

sec.title: PK of total radioactivity, valemetostat, and CALZ-1809a in the plasma

sec.p: The median Tmax for total radioactivity, valemetostat, and CALZ-1809a in the plasma was 2.5 (range, 1.5–5.0), 2.5 (1.5–5.0), and 4.0 (2.0–5.0) hours, respectively. While most participants (6/8) demonstrated rapid absorption of valemetostat within ≤ 3.0 h, two participants had slightly extended absorption phases of 4.0 and 5.0 h. The median Tmax for CALZ-1809a was approximately 1.5 h following the Tmax for valemetostat. The mean (SD) t1/2 for total radioactivity, valemetostat, and CALZ-1809a was 17.2 (6.90), 12.7 (2.71), and 61.2 (19.2) hours, respectively, with plasma concentrations declining generally in a biphasic manner in all groups. The total radioactivity was quantifiable in plasma up to 72 h post-dose in four participants, while for valemetostat, the last quantifiable concentrations were measured between 36 and 72 h post-dose. CALZ-1809a was still measurable in one participant until 360 h post-dose (The lower limit of quantitation was 20 ng/mL and 1 ng/mL for valemetostat and CALZ-1809a, respectively).

The mean (SD) AUCinf ratio for plasma valemetostat/total radioactivity and plasma CALZ-1809a/valemetostat was 0.55 (0.10) and 0.88 (0.27), respectively. At almost all time points, the total molar concentrations of valemetostat and CALZ-1809a in plasma were > 80% of total plasma radioactivity.

In whole blood, the median Tmax was similar to the plasma at 2.75 h. Radioactivity levels declined in a biphasic manner, with a slightly lower mean t1/2 (SD) of 11.8 (2.81) hours than with plasma. Radioactivity was quantifiable up to 36 h post-dose in four participants. The coefficient of variation percentages of Cmax and AUCinf in the whole blood were 21.7% and 24.4%, respectively. Figure 2 demonstrates the concentration time profiles of total radioactivity in whole blood and plasma.

sec.title: Identification and structural characterization of metabolites
sec.p: In the pooled plasma biological samples, almost complete radioactivity (≥ 95.8%) was extracted, reconstituted, and recovered from the column.

Radioactivity column recoveries for Plasma 1 and Plasma 2 samples were 155.4% and 117.0%, respectively and radioactivity recovered from urine and fecal samples ranged from 93.0 to 168.4%. Column recovery was high (> 110%) in some samples, likely because the injected radioactivity was low, and the recovery was largely affected by the background value.

In pooled plasma samples, valemetostat, CALZ-1809a, and two other metabolites were detected. Valemetostat accounted for 95.9% of the total radioactivity in pooled plasma samples from various participants at Cmax (Plasma 2). CALZ-1809a accounted for 1.1% of the total radioactivity, M1 for 1.0%, and M5 for 1.3%. When the radioactivity was measured in pooled samples in a participant across multiple time points (Plasma 1), valemetostat accounted for 77.1% of the total radioactivity, CALZ-1809a for 14.9%, and M1 for 6.7%.

The metabolite profiles of the urine and feces are shown in Table 1 and the cumulative excretions of radioactivity are shown in Supplementary Table 3. In urine samples, valemetostat, CALZ-1809a, and five other metabolites were detected. The mean cumulative radioactive dose recovery for unchanged valemetostat was at 10.0% of the dose. The metabolite identified at the highest concentration was M6 (1.75%). Metabolite M1 was detected at 1.14%, and all other metabolites identified were < 1% of the dose.

In fecal samples, valemetostat, CALZ-1809a, and five other metabolites were detected. The mean cumulative radioactive dose recovery was at 64.9% for valemetostat and 5.61% for M4 (CALZ-1809a). Metabolites M7, M8, and M9 (CALZ-1810a) were detected at 1.66%, 1.26%, and 1.64% of the radioactive dose, respectively, and all other metabolites represented < 1% of the dose.

Radiochromatograms of biological samples are demonstrated in Fig. 3. Mass chromatograms of authentic standards and corresponding biological samples acquired with LC–MS are shown in Supplementary Fig. 2. The proposed metabolic pathways of valemetostat are shown in Fig. 4. Valemetostat was identified in the biological samples with retention times, accurate masses of corresponding [M + H]+, and fragmentation patterns equivalent to the valemetostat authentic standard. Metabolite M1 had an m/z of 680, corresponding to C32H43ClN3O11, and their product ions were observed at m/z of 504, 365, 353, 328, 316, and 152. The metabolite was proposed to be a glucuronide of oxidized valemetostat at dimethylpyridinone. Metabolite M2 had an m/z of 353, corresponding to C18H25ClN2O3, and its product ions were observed at m/z of 308, 226, and 202. The retention times, the accurate masses of corresponding [M + H]+, and fragmentation patterns were equivalent with those of the authentic reference standard (CALZ-1808a). Metabolite M3 had an m/z of 522, corresponding to C26H36ClN3O6, and their product ions were observed at m/z of 504 and 336. The metabolite was proposed to be a dihydrodiol of valemetostat at dimethylpyridinone. Metabolite M4 was confirmed to be CALZ-1809a, with retention times, accurate masses of corresponding [M + H]+, and fragmentation patterns equivalent to the CALZ-1809a authentic standard. Metabolite M5 had an m/z of 520, corresponding to C26H35ClN3O6, and the product ions were observed at m/z of 502, 393, and 336. The metabolite was proposed to be valemetostat dioxidized at dimethylpyridinone. Metabolite M6 had an m/z of 650, corresponding to C32H44ClN3O9, and its product ions were observed at m/z 340. This metabolite was proposed to be a glucose conjugate of valemetostat at dimethylpyridinone. Metabolite M7 had an m/z of 520, corresponding to C26H35ClN3O6, and its product ions were observed at m/z of 502, 393, and 336. This metabolite was proposed to be valemetostat dioxidized at dimethylpyridinone. Metabolite M8 had an m/z of 520, corresponding to C26H35ClN3O6, and its product ions were observed at m/z of 502, 393, and 336. This metabolite was proposed to be valemetostat dioxidized at dimethylpyridinone. Metabolite M9 had an m/z of 474, corresponding to C25H33ClN3O4 and its product ions were observed at m/z of 339, 322, 136, and 124. The retention times, the accurate masses of corresponding [M + H]+, and fragmentation patterns were equivalent with those of the authentic reference standard (CALZ-1810a). Metabolite M10 had an m/z of 649, corresponding to C31H42ClN4O7S and was proposed to be an N-acetyl cysteine conjugate of valemetostat. The proposed structure was estimated from the accurate mass and expected composition formula because the product ions could not be observed.

sec.title: Plasma protein, albumin, and AAG binding
sec.p: The binding of valemetostat 600–10,000 ng/mL to plasma, 4% HSA, and 0.1% AAG was studied by LC–MS/MS analyses. Full valemetostat protein binding results are shown in Supplementary Table 4. Valemetostat was highly bound to plasma (> 94%) at 600 and 3,000 ng/mL and decreased to 78.0% at 10,000 ng/mL. The binding of valemetostat to AAG was high (92.3%) at 600 ng/mL and decreased with increasing valemetostat concentration until a binding percentage of 56.0% at 10,000 ng/mL. The percentage of valemetostat bound to 4% HSA was concentration-independent and ranged from 35.0 to 38.7%.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this study, the single dose of 200 mg of [14C]-valemetostat administered to eight healthy male participants was safe and well tolerated, with only one TEAE of Grade 1 diarrhea considered related to treatment.

[14C]-valemetostat was approximately 95% recovered (15.6% in urine and 79.8% in feces) after a single oral administration of the radioactive dose, indicating that the absorption, metabolism, and disposition of valemetostat were well characterized. Valemetostat elimination primarily occurred by fecal excretion, with 86.7% of radioactivity recovered (15.3% in urine, 71.4% in feces) within the first 96 h of the oral dose. Unchanged valemetostat accounted for 10.0% and 64.9% of the administered radioactive dose in urine and feces, respectively. CALZ-1809a (M4), an oxidized metabolite of valemetostat, was the major metabolite identified and was present in all biological samples. CALZ-1809a accounted for 1.14% and 5.61% of the total radioactivity in the urine and feces, respectively. Five other compounds were each detected in urine (M1, M2, M3, M5, and M6) and feces (M3, M7, M8, M9, and M10) as minor metabolites at less than 2% abundance. Metabolite identification suggested that valemetostat is mainly metabolized by oxidation, and to a lesser extent, by various routes of conjugation.

Following a single oral administration, valemetostat was rapidly absorbed into the systemic circulation, with the median Tmax occurring at 2.5 h post-dose in the plasma for both radioactivity and the unchanged valemetostat. After reaching Cmax, plasma concentrations generally declined in a biphasic manner with a mean t1/2 of 17.2 and 12.7 h for total radioactivity and valemetostat, respectively. The blood to plasma ratio of AUCinf for total radioactivity was 0.54, suggesting that valemetostat and its metabolites resided mainly in the plasma and were minimally associated with red blood cells. The systemic exposure of total radioactivity in the plasma was higher compared to unchanged valemetostat by approximately 20% for Cmax, and 45% for AUCinf, suggesting that metabolites contributed considerably to the total radioactivity measured.

In plasma, three metabolites (M1, M4, and M5) were identified. CALZ-1809a (M4) was the major circulating metabolite of valemetostat and had a long t1/2 (61.2 h). The mean (SD) AUCinf ratio for plasma CALZ-1809a/ valemetostat was 0.88 (0.27). At almost all time points, the total molar concentrations of valemetostat and CALZ-1809a in the plasma were > 80% of total plasma radioactivity. In vitro studies have previously demonstrated that CALZ-1809a is formed by CYP3A enzymes and has approximately a 24-fold and 4.3-fold weaker inhibitory activity than valemetostat on EZH1 and EZH2, respectively (IC50 values for EZH1: CALZ-1809a, 0.24 µM vs. valemetostat, 0.010 µM; IC50 values for EZH2: CALZ-1809a, 0.026 µM vs. valemetostat, 0.006 µM [Data on file]), and has higher protein binding affinity (Data on file). Therefore, the contribution to an in vivo pharmacological effect by CALZ-1809a is considered to be low.

In vitro, valemetostat exhibited a high degree of protein binding in a concentration-dependent manner in human plasma, with a greater binding affinity to AAG than to HSA. AAG is an acute-phase protein upregulated in inflammatory and disease conditions, including malignancies such as NHLs [19]. The mean (SD) baseline AAG concentration in healthy participants was 70 (13.27) mg/dL (N = 8; Supplementary Table 2), which is comparable to the levels observed in healthy individuals in a previous valemetostat population PK analysis (53.4 [16.4] mg/dL; n = 72) but lower than those reported in patients with NHL in the same analysis (99.3 [41.0] mg/dL; n = 102) [14]. The population PK study identified AAG levels as the most influential covariate for total valemetostat exposure, likely due to the high protein binding of valemetostat. Whereas AAG levels were shown to have a minimal impact on unbound (free) valemetostat exposure, suggesting that elevated AAG levels in patients with NHLs are unlikely to affect the efficacy and safety of valemetostat [14]. As there is a large variation in AAG levels amongst individuals, valemetostat protein binding likely contributes to the significant inter-individual variability observed in previous valemetostat PK studies [13, 20].

In summary, this study demonstrated that valemetostat is rapidly absorbed following oral administration to healthy participants under fasting conditions. Most of the administered radioactive dose was excreted via the biliary/fecal route mainly as unchanged valemetostat, and to a lesser extent, as oxidative or conjugated metabolites. The major circulating metabolite was a hydroxylated valemetostat (CALZ-1809a) formed by CYP3A enzymes. Valemetostat is highly bound to plasma protein, and AAG is the most abundant species.
